title: "Shooting" 9V battery; what causes it?
body:
This question is somewhat off-topic, and maybe it would better fit in Chemistry, but still I think it fits here somehow, so read on.

This is a true story (a bit long, sorry): A few days ago while I was working on my computer, I suddenly heard a loud noise like an exploding light bulb with a specific sound of glass being hit. So I turned around, investigating. As the light bulb was LED only, it was looking OK. There were just two more electrical devices, but they looked OK as well, but there was a slight "electric smell", so I suspected an exploding electrolytic capacitor, but still the noise wouldn't fit unless something shot out of an enclosure.

Finding nothing I gave up after a while, but still being worried slightly what may have broken. A few days later I found this on the floor, first thinking it's some small nail that had fallen off the wall, but there wasn't a nail in the wall.

So I felt assured that it was the positive pole of an exploded electrolytic capacitor, but still I couldn't find where it came from.

Then two days later I saw this 9V battery hidden under a pile of paper:

Obviously something came out from the bottom with quite some energy (I could not find the missing part), and then I had an explanation: One of the battery cells exploded, breaking the plastic on the bottom and shooting out at high speed about three meters, then hitting the glass of the room lamp. The other end of the battery looked similar, most likely damaged by the recoil of the explosion:

Seen from the side it looked like this:

So if you ever wondered why the battery industry seems unable to manufacture batteries that do not leak, this may be the reason: If batteries don't leak, they will explode!

So we are at the main question:

What happens inside a battery that is either old, or depleted (empty)? Obviously some type of gas develops that either squeezes some of the substances out (as most batteries do), or causes the battery to explode.

title: Why does the powerline frequency have anything to do with TV framerate?
body:
Sorry if this isn't the right place to ask this, but I couldn't think of a better one.

It's a well-known fact that NTSC television runs at 60 fields per second, and that PAL runs at 50 fields per second. The oft-cited reason for this is that the American electrical grid runs at 60Hz, and the European one runs at 50Hz. My question is why these should have anything to do with each other.

Obviously, televisions are universally plugged into electrical outlets (or were at the time NTSC and PAL were being developed), and therefore have access to a reliable 50Hz or 60Hz signal that they could e.g. use as the input to a PLL or similar. There is no reason to expect, however, that the zero cross of the power line will coincide with the vertical blanking interval of the TV signal. Even if the local broadcasting station synchronized their cameras to the powerline frequency, the difference in distance between the straight shot from the TV transmitter tower to the antenna and the long, winding path of the power poles would introduce an appreciable enough speed-of-light delay to throw it out of alignment, surely? The TV would have to have additional circuitry to detect the vertical blanking interval and find the appropriate delay between it and the power line to figure out where in the frame it should be based on the power line, wouldn't it?

Having been born after the towers fell, I wasn't around for the earliest TV sets, but the videos I've seen of them on YouTube seem to suggest they have a knob on the back that adjusts the frequency of some internal oscillator controlling the vertical interval, completely independently of the power line. Were there even earlier sets (or more inexpensive sets) that didn't have this oscillator and relied on the power line somehow? If so, how did they synchronize that with the TV signal?

title: In a series circuit, does the first component briefly receive full voltage before the electric field propagates?
body:
I’m struggling to reconcile the idea of voltage division in a series circuit with how the electric field propagates when a circuit is first energized. Here’s my confusion:

Scenario: A DC circuit with two lamps in series and a battery. When the switch is flipped, the electric field propagates at near-light speed, but not instantaneously.

Quastion: At the exact moment the field reaches the first lamp but hasn’t yet reached the second lamp, isn’t the first lamp temporarily exposed to the full battery voltage?

Explanation: When the field has only push through the area before the first lamp and in between the first lamp and second lamp, then the circuit in this very instant is basically voltage supply > lamp > ground right? I know there is no ground connected between the second lamp and first lamp, but the short wire should act like a ground before the electric field passes through it right? Just like a wire of infinite length can act just like a ground?

I’m told voltage splits instantly because the electric field “sees” the entire circuit. But since there is a delay(despite it's so short that no one is gonna notice), doesn’t the first lamp briefly act as the sole load? I mean just because it happens and finish almost instantly doesn't mean it does not exist right?

Update: Here is what I thought. The only thing required to light up a lamp is a flowing current. As we know that current is basically flow of electron, which moves very very very slowly from - to +, the reason that the entire circuit can have current almost instantly is that electric field flies in the speed of light and all the electron it reaches will form current, so the currents are generated by the electric field as it passes from + to -. Therefore the lamp touched by the electric field at first will light up first.

title: Hole in fuse + damage to PCB when fuse blows, why?
body:
Short version:

Why did my fuses blow with holes in them and ejecting something on the PCB?

Long version:

For the second time in a few month, I observed fuse "failures", where the fuse, instead of just "blowing" (in the sense becoming open) also pierced and ejected something (molten sand?) that also blackened the PCB and damaged one or 2 fuses next to it.

Some images:

recent failure (F8 blew, and damaged F7 (also open circuit)):

Both fuses are open circuit. F8 has a hole (2*3mm) in it. F7 is cracked (NB: F7 is a different type of fuse: glass, not ceramic). The holders seem molten on the right side (between F7 and F8).

Older failure (fault downstream of F5; F6 and F7 also failed):

Fuse F5 (3 small holes, cracked, holder massively molten to the point of soldering to the fuse):

Fuses F5 (front), F6 and F7 (F6 cracked and small hole); all 3 open circuit with molten holder (F5 the most, F7 the least)

The system:

  • voltage: 320 VDC nominal (I never measured more than 322 VDC, lower voltage under high load due to long cable losses (8ohms))
  • global current: the voltage source is a CC/CV power supply, with limits set at 320 VDC and 30 A
  • loads: each fuse protects the wiring to a brushless DC motor with internal control electronics, rated for 4.5 A max at full speed. Due to internal control, I haven't seen any inrush current in excess of 4.5 A
  • ambient temperature in the electronics enclosure: somewhere between 15 and 50°C (I don't have the records of temperature when the fuse failed)

The fuses:

  • Bussmann BK1-S505H-5-R
  • 5 A
  • time-delay
  • rated 400 VDC / 600 VAC
  • fuse holder: 3518P

Cause of failures:

Short circuit in the load (failure of the IGBTs, creating a low resistance path). In the newer failure it was on the load connected to F8, in the older one it was on the load connected to F5. For the newer failure, it happened at power on, current <10 mA nominally in each load before the failure (I have no data for the older failure).

Details of the PCB:

Schematics 1/2:

Schematics 2/2:

Layout: layer 1 (320 VDC; traces = 1.8 mm):

Layout: layers 2 and 3 (they are identical): earth ; traces = 5 mm except last bit = 1.8 mm:

Layout: layer 4 (bottom): 0 VDC; traces = 5 mm except last bit = 1.8 mm

NB: this is a legacy PCB, not idea why there are not continuous planes for earth and 0 VDC (excepted where clearance is needed), nor why the 320 VDC traces are so small.

I have tried reproducing the failures at 10 or 20 A fault currents (shorting the load and setting the supply to 10/20 A and 20 V max), without success (i.e. the fuse blew, but without any external damage).

Questions:

Why did the fuses fail in this way (i.e. with a hole in it, and ejecting something (molten sand?))?

How can I reproduce this on purpose?

What should I change to prevent it from occurring again?

EDIT: in regard of @AndyAka's answer and Jen's comment, it seems that the capacitors might play a significant role, so here is extra information about them (NB: it's not the same model for the 2 PCBs).

Recent failure MAL225977221E3:

  • 220 µF
  • ESR = 0.269R typ @ 100 Hz, 0.123R typ@ 300 Hz, 0.56R max at 100 Hz, 0.4R max @10 kHz

Older failure 861221486019:

  • 220 µF
  • ESR = 1.21R max @ 120 Hz

So in case of a dead short, with two capacitors in parallel, the current might exceed the 1500 A rating of the fuse.

The power supply, on the other hand, is separated from this PCB by 300 m of cable, with about 8 ohms resistance, so even if the supply has a lot of output capacitance, it can't contribute more than 320/8 = 40 A even for a short duration.

title: Regulator blowing up. Does it need more protection?
body:
I had some PCBs manufactured for work recently, but for whatever reason the power circuit occasionally fails. What happens is that after the board is connected to a DC +24V power supply, the regulator sometimes lets out the magic smoke and the 3.3V output gets shorted to GND.

This will only sometimes happen when the board is connected to an already-powered benchtop power supply, so my suspicion is that it is caused by a voltage spike from the power supply as it is connected. Note that it doesn't always happen and there are several boards that haven't been blown up.

The schematic for the power circuit is shown below:

The datasheet for the 3.3V regulator (TS30042) can be found here.
The datasheet for the varistor (V33MLA1206H) at the input can be found here.
C20 is Yageo CC0603MRY5V9BB104. This is a 100nF 50V Y5V 0603 capacitor.
C22 is Murata GRM188R6YA106MA73#. This is a 10uF 35V X5R 0603 capacitor.

The main loads that it has to power are an ESP32 (using WiFi Tx/Rx) and an RFM95 module, so I might expect it to get up to 1A, but that's just a quick estimate.

The layout of the PCB does not closely follow the guidelines in the regulator's datasheet. However, I can't imagine that would lead the to the regulator blowing up, right?

This board is a 4 layer board. This image shows the top layer, bottom layer, and GND plane. The power plane is split between U5 and C20. The bottom half is the +24V net which also connects to other some switchable outputs. The +3V3 net goes from the below U5 to the rest of the board. This does mean there are only two thin traces connecting the 24V input to the regulator.

Finally, here's a picture of the blown regulator. Pin 1 is the top pin on the left side, with pin numbers increasing anti-clockwise. It may be hard to tell in the image, but there are burn holes on the top of the package next to pins 2/3 and pin 11, which are the pins input pins that are connected to 24V. This seems to be true for all burnt out chips.

As I mentioned, the output (3.3V) of the chip gets shorted to GND. If I remove the chip, the 3.3V line is no longer shorted, so it seems that the fault is localised to the regulator and nothing else is faulty. And even if it was caused by a short circuit somewhere else, the regulator's datasheet claims that it has overcurrent and thermal protection. No other components are visually damaged either.

Is this likely to be caused by a voltage spike when connecting to the power supply? If so, how should this be prevented? Would it be better to replace the varistor with a TVS diode? Or is the varistor not spec'd correctly?

title: Why use a 1000:1 transformer instead cascading three 10:1 transformers?
body:
I was researching different ways to make a high voltage DC-DC power supply in the 20 kV ~ 30 kV range, with output of a few tens of micro amps. The purpose is for testing isolation and resistance to ESD on panel mount components.

One common factor I seem to run across in the DIY electronics world is people using transformers with very high turns ratios. They can't be made by hand and are often salvaged from old CRT monitors/TVs. While that works for a one-off design, it's not really suitable for designing a reproducible product.

Why not just use several transformers in series with lower turns ratios instead of one transformer with a very high turns ratio? For example, instead of using a 1000:1 transformer, use three 10:1 transformers.

10:1 transformers can pretty easily be wound by hand. It's likely cheaper to make (at least from a coil winding standpoint), and as a bonus you get multiple stages of isolation between your input and output.

I am sure there is some practical reason for it, but it's not yet obvious to me.

I'm proceeding forward on a simple instrument design to quickly characterize small signal bipolar transistors, both NPN and PNP, for three key parameters: saturation current (\$I_{\small{SAT}}\$), emission co-efficient or non-ideality factor (\$\eta\$), and DC current gain (\$h_{\small{FE}}\$ or \$\beta_{\small{F}}\$):

editable schematic

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

or an easier-to-access image

I want to use a common \$9\:\text{V}\$ battery for the project. The JFET inputs are helpful here, and the TL082 device is cheap. And TI's equally cheap H version sports a very low \$1\:\text{pA}\$ bias. There's a lot that can be done to improve the design. And I may need to, if testing experience demands it. But a week into it, and so far, the results are promising.

The COTS panel meters are nice. I've tested all five of those I've received, and they consistently exhibit almost exactly \$1.23\:\text{M}\Omega\$ input resistance, regardless of the supply rail voltage. I tested with a variety of supply voltages and used them to measure a variety of voltages, and all five of them always come out at \$1.23\:\text{M}\Omega\$. The impedance doesn't vary with the signal being measured.

(The panel meters also all burn between \$16\:\text{mA}\$ and \$17\:\text{mA}\$, also independent of the battery source voltage I use. Since they are spec'd to operate from anything between \$4\:\text{V}\$ (though they run more dimly on \$3\:\text{V}\$) and \$28\:\text{V}\$, it would substantially aid the \$9\:\text{V}\$ battery if I added a switcher to produce \$4\:\text{V}\$. But that can be deferred as an improved version, should I decide to care enough about it. I'd have to spend time that I cannot afford right now, digging through the weeds to find something that is designed to work off a \$9\:\text{V}\$ alkaline battery and for a \$20\:\text{mA}\$ compliance. (A quick scan on Digikey and I saw most targeting much higher currents.) Or I could just run the display off of a separate Infinity X1 rechargeable, for example. But I'm joking about that -- being a \$9\:\text{V}\$ alkaline battery project is a requirement, and it is working fine, and the draw requirements are squarely within the targeted devices for such alkaline batteries.)

What I'm doing now for that calibration potentiometer and why I want to change

For now, I've been using about two feet of #30 wire-wrap wire from OK industries. I just make it too long and then cut bits of it off until the meter zeros out perfectly. Then I'm done.

But I expect drift. And I'd like to prepare something that others can consider doing and using. (No one may care. And that's okay, if so. But I'd like to at least smooth the road a bit, just in case.) They should be able to adjust the potentiometer from time to time, when calibrating the meter for zero. (There's a switch position to gain access to the LM4040 reference for gain calibration purposes.) One could just write it down and subtract it every time. But I'm finding it a bit annoying, and I'm sure others may, as well.

The offset I've found in the meters is consistently positive and shows up as between \$3\:\text{mV}\$ to about \$4\:\text{mV}\$. It's not much. But it is several counts of the second least significant digit. And it just looks better to get a nice stable zero out.

For the #30 gauge wire, the "resolution" needed is about one inch. Anything finer than that probably isn't needed. This means a resolution of about \$5\:\text{m}\Omega\$ would be more than enough. Probably \$10\:\text{m}\Omega\$ would be fine. But no worse than that. And it should not feel as though you just can't get it down to the pixel so to speak. It should be easy to zero the meter without dealing with physical hand-jitter, making it too painful a process to get it accidentally "just right."

Obviously, two feet of #30 bare copper with a sliding clip works. Been there, done that. But it would be a lot bigger than the board, and it is hard to tuck it into the project box, later, without all that bare copper touching something awkward.

Finer wire starts to become too easily broken, I think. But I am currently working through ideas like that, which can be simply mounted on the board. A slider bar style mechanism on stand-offs would be okay.

Perhaps consider a way of using the copper-clad surface of the board itself? Or some other idea that can be mounted on said board using the above construction technique and fabricated by a hobbyist.

A serpentine trace going around and around the board came to mind. But even if I could figure out a clip for it, I can't imagine anyone wanting to use their exacto knife for that mission.

I'm looking for construction ideas to explore that would fit well into this specific project, be easy to make and use, and serve the purpose.

The device is working very nicely. But this meter zeroing is my current problem in front of me, and I'm open to ideas to try.

Motes

It is a requirement that this be a \$9\:\text{V}\$ alkaline battery project. That's immutable.

For the current version-0 project, it is also a requirement that parts count is kept as low as possible, consistent with maintaining functionality, low cost, and part availability.

This means that I don't use a switcher IC to produce a lower voltage for the COTS voltmeter, despite the benefits. Or negative voltage rails.

In the next version, the door is open to a switcher IC in order to gain reduced draw from the battery by using a lower voltage for the COTs meter. (Or, alternatively, find a COTS voltmeter that is a transflective LCD display with 5 digits and can replace the one I am using now.) If it turns out that the next version goes in the direction of a switcher IC, it may then also be in the cards to consider generating a negative rail.

The panel meter I'm using really is quite good. One count in the least digit is \$100\:\mu\text{V}\$. But it's not a noisy digit. Given a precision voltage, it will sit there quite precisely. And if I place my hand onto the circuit being measured to alter the voltage (touch a transistor and stuff moves pretty fast!) it will see it. When I remove my hand, it settles right back to the exact same place. So I'm developing some serious respect for the COTS device that I hadn't been sure of earlier.

What this means for calibrating it down to zero is that as one gets closer, then it will show 5 digits of 0 and then either a - or + with one digit changing for a moment. This repeats at some rate. But when I nail the zero correctly, it does not move around. It also does not move around when I change the power supply voltage from \$4\:\text{V}\$ to \$19\:\text{V}\$, for example. Despite the excess heat that must be going on. And I have let this set on the table for an hour. No motion.

I'm just liking this particular unit, so far.

When I above write about "cut in one inch" pieces, then test, then another inch, etc., note that this reflects a change of about \$7\:\text{m}\Omega\$. That seemed to work okay for the five times I did this calibration step. But keep in mind the \$17\:\text{mA}\$ draw. With \$100\:\mu\text{V}\$ per count in the least digit, I get \$\frac{100\:\mu\text{V}}{17\:\text{mA}}\approx 5.9\:\text{m}\Omega\$. If the least digit is toggling back and forth around zero, but not settling on it, that means I'm getting very close. Then, fixing it means maybe not going by more than a \$50\:\mu\text{V}\$ shift to avoid completely skipping over the null point to the other side.

The solution I've been using works very well. It's almost free and requires very little board change. And I've had no problems with it. It's just awkward.

A 3" long stretch of #32 platinum wire, together with a grabber clip, would seem viable:

But it's not a solution I'm looking for here.

The platinum wire would be USD12, right now. (And the Pomona 72902 is double that much!)

(I'm still going to buy some and test it just because I'm curious.)

Closing the question -- selecting an answer

In the process of testing out some of the ideas expressed in the answers -- and I cannot fully express my profound appreciation that goes out to everyone on that score -- I've found that the better-working approach remains, by far, uses the original very small adjustment approach. It's taken a lot of testing to see it, and my apologies for that delay.

I've also uncovered a possible need for yet another parameter for matching discrete pairs that I need to spend still more time on. So I'm closing this question. I've received far more than I deserved. I will +1 all the answers -- all of them were constructive. The selected answer is simply the one I feel contributed more to altering my testing directions over recent days.

title: BGA ball collapse visible in X-ray — could this be caused by electrical overstress (24 V input pads)?
body:
I’m analyzing a BGA failure on a board and I'm trying to determine whether the damaged solder balls seen in X-ray come from thermal fatigue or from a more sudden electrical overstress (EOS) / overcurrent event.

Below are the X-ray images (I can post more if needed). Two balls show a very irregular and collapsed shape, with clear loss of spherical geometry and internal material displacement.

Images:

What I observe:

  • The affected balls are collapsed internally, not just voided.
  • Shape is asymmetric, with material shifted to one side.
  • This does not look like a typical void or cold joint.
  • Impact is localized — only 1–2 balls are affected, the rest of the array looks normal.

Important detail:

The defective solder balls are located exactly on the pads that receive the 24 V input to the device. This makes me suspect the following possibilities:

1. Electrical Overstress (EOS)

A sudden overcurrent or transient could rapidly heat the ball internally, causing collapse or partial melting.

2. Short-circuit event

If the BGA experienced a momentary short on the 24 V rail, it might generate a very fast and localized thermal spike.

3. Thermal fatigue?

Possible, but typical thermal fatigue often creates:

  • Cracks (linear, interfacial)
  • Gas-like voids
  • More gradual failure across multiple balls

Here the damage looks much more violent and localized, more consistent with EOS.

My questions:

  1. Does this X-ray pattern look consistent with electrical overstress / overcurrent damage on BGA solder balls?
  2. Can a 24 V transient or short realistically cause this type of collapse inside just a single ball?
  3. Are there known failure signatures in X-ray that clearly differentiate EOS from thermal cycling fatigue?
  4. Is there anything else I should inspect (die attach, PCB pad integrity, intermetallic layer, current path, etc.)?

Additional context:

  • Lead-free SAC solder (likely SAC305)
  • No evidence of global overheating of the PCB
  • Only the 24 V input balls show deformation
  • The device stopped working after an unknown event in the system
  • No mechanical stress was applied to the board

What I’m looking for:

Guidance from people with experience in:

  • BGA X-ray interpretation
  • Failure analysis (FA) / reliability
  • EOS / ESD / overcurrent events
  • High-power electronics
  • Any insight or reference images would be extremely helpful.

title: How to improve discrete active rectifier circuit
body:
This circuit is commonly seen, a simple active rectifier:

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

Just showing the half-wave version here, as it's also convenient to breadboard. I've added source resistance explicitly (R4), and a current shunt (R3) to measure rectification action.

It seems to work alright (V2 set for 8Vpk):

But it has a dark side:

Q1 Vebo is easily exceeded!

This is easily proven out on the breadboard:

10x probes, so the measurements are 1/10. Ch2: AC, Ch3: IS.

V1 is 3.18V, R4 = 51Ω, and V2 turned up just high enough to tease breakdown. Evidently this 2N3904 breaks down at 8.9V. Notice the ominous (nominally-)off-state bump upward in current, just right of middle. (Also, yes, the mains waveform is a bit flat-topped here. That makes it a little harder to distinguish rectification or breakdown from normal waveform, unfortunately.)

Switching performance is good, at least: even with this rather large MOSFET operated at such low (forward and pull-up) currents, effective reverse recovery is nonexistent up to 30kHz (using a function generator instead of transformer to supply it). Forward recovery is quite noticeable though, taking about 50µs to stabilize to 200mV "Vf" at 100mA If for example. (Simple enough to address: R2 could be reduced, or an emitter follower used to drive M1 more strongly.)

We could change 2N3904 to 2N7000 (a fairly drastic change, but actually no other circuit changes needed here), which is rated for 18V Vgs(max). But this merely shifts the goalposts: what if we needed 30V, or 300V? (Well okay, 300V is well in the domain where SiC schottky look attractive -- but, one could always be in search of just a little bit more efficiency, so why not?) What about transient immunity? (In full-wave doubler and bridge configurations, transient voltage is clamped to supply voltage (plus a small margin) by body diodes, but FWCT and half-wave are still worth considering.)

Using MOSFETs presents its own problem: the simulation (I'm not going to repeat it here but the reader is welcome to give it a try) doesn't know that bogey 2N7000s (any discrete MOSFETs, generally) don't match; you have to modify the model(s) manually.

Just grabbing a random pair of 2N7000s here, they measure Vgs(th) = 2.012V and 1.958V. Pretty close (much tighter than the datasheet range of 1 to 3V!), but enough to see a difference. With them in one orientation, I see:

Seems alright, but swapped around and zoomed in a bit, we see:

Showing two "strength" levels (R4 = 51Ω (black), 15Ω (pink)). The timings are similar, suggesting a reverse recovery effect; and the time scale (~40µs) might even be construed as dynamic (corresponding to the forward recovery measured above). But that doesn't check out: turn-off is much sharper on account of Q2 shunting M1's Qg; only turn-on is mediated by R2 pull-up. (This is borne out by G waveform, not shown here. Waveforms appear quasi-static at this frequency. Again, 10s of kHz were necessary to make "forward recovery" due to R2 evident, and this does not depend on Q1/Q2 type.)

Rather, what happens is the "diode" remains "on" in reverse. Surprisingly, despite the spread of 54mV, this blip is only around 4 or 8mV (which should be even less at the MOSFETs, considering IRFIZ34G's Rds(on) is much less than R3)

A diode staying "on" is a peculiar diode at the very least, but given that the total spread for 2N7000 is 2V, it could very well remain "on" until -2V -- in many applications, it might simply never reach such voltage at all and stay shorted instead!

Incidentally, matched BJTs are available -- not monolithic, not abundantly or cheaply -- but informally matched (e.g. from the same wafer) dice, packaged together, are reasonably common and quite cheap. I'm not aware of any such equivalent for MOSFETs; discrete MOSFET circuits just aren't as good as BJT, anyway, and for as few remaining applications that use discretes, it's no surprise the MOSFET equivalent doesn't exist. (Yes, there are the matched, monolithic, zero-threshold, programmable, etc. parts by ALD -- which, as with monolithic BJTs, are boutique parts: available, but you aren't going to use them at any kind of scale, not unless you really, really need to.)

In summary, both presented alternatives have significant drawbacks:

  • BJTs, while they perform well dynamically, and are available in good matching, Vebo is a significant disadvantage to operating voltage range, and transient immunity in non-self-clamped configurations
  • MOSFET's equivalent Vgs(max) limit is only a few times higher, and have very poor matching

What techniques can be employed to address these issues?

title: What Exactly Does “Linearity” Mean for Passive Components Like Inductors and Capacitors?

title: Circuit for wiping / destroying IC on a smart card
body:

Background

I think the idea is to make sure that those ICs are properly disposed off.

Thus, since we are talking about credit cards, bank cards, health care provider cards etc. I'm looking for simple ways to wipe the chips before dropping the cards off.

title: How can boost converter li-ion 9V batteries achieve low self discharge?
body:
I bought several li-ion 9V boost converter batteries intended to replace 9V alkalines, chargeable with USB-C. These batteries have a 1 Ah 3.6 .. 3.7 V li-ion cell and a boost converter creating constant 9V voltage over the entire discharge range. Useful for powering electronics that need 9V voltage.

This is a different approach than 7 NiMH cells in series (8.4 V nominal), or 2 li-ion cells in series (8.4 V full, 7.2 or 7.4 V nominal), or 3 LiFePO4 cells in series (9.6 V nominal, the full charge voltage may be limited to avoid breaking electronics that are designed for 9V alkalines).

The manufacturer stated 300 mAh minimum capacity at 9V voltage, and less than 2% / month self discharge at 20 degrees Celsius.

Because these batteries have a boost converter, I'm somewhat curious about how it's possible to achieve 2% / month self discharge, and whether the self discharge is low only when idle, or also when there's very small continuous drain by a device that's "off" but still consumes some minimal current.

How can these batteries achieve less than 2% / month self discharge?

edit ---

Here's some measurements:

Discharge capacity was 0.301 Ah, 2.629 Wh at 0.1 A current (which translates to about 0.750 Ah at 3.6 V). Charging back at 5V took 0.966 Ah or 4.936 Wh. This suggests the charging circuit may be using a low dropout linear regulator as opposed to a buck converter, given the very low grid-to-device efficiency.

I measured the switching noise of the circuit with an oscilloscope by using a 1 Mohm / 10 Mohm probe:

  • With 10 Mohm probe, the noise had sawtooth shape with 0.78 kHz frequency (1.28 ms cycle time)
  • With 1 Mohm probe, the noise had sawtooth shape with 1.4 kHz frequency (0.7 ms cycle time)
  • With 100 kohm additional resistor in parallel with 1 Mohm probe, the noise had sawtooth shape with 1.67 kHz frequency (0.6 ms cycle time)
  • With 10 kohm additional resistor in parallel with 1 Mohm probe, the noise started to look more like a triangle wave, but the rise time was markedly shorter than the fall time, with 3.70 kHz frequency (0.27 ms cycle time)
  • With 1 kohm additional resistor in parallel with 1 Mohm probe, the noise was triangle wave with somewhat unequal rise and fall times, with 22.7 kHz frequency (44 µs cycle time).

I don't have a 100X probe, but I assume the frequency wouldn't probably drop much below 0.78 kHz at 100 Mohm.

So, the device is clearly using a boost converter that is alternately turned on and off. There's probably large output capacitance, and the boost converter is switched on when the output voltage reaches a threshold low voltage, and switched off when the output voltage reaches a threshold high voltage. This explains the rather low self discharge: the boost converter is most of the time switched off, it isn't continuously operating.

The 300 mAh capacity at 100 kohm resistance would be about 15 months, and at 1 Mohm resistance 150 months. With 100 kohm, the frequency is about twice that of when idle (10 Mohm). With less than 2% self discharge per month, the self discharge would happen in 50 months.

-- /edit

title: Does a resistor in series with an LED draw more power than a resistor alone?
body:
Basically the title, but I wanted to check my intuition and math on the subject here, just to be sure.

If I have a 10 V source, a 1kΩ resistor, and an LED with a \$V_{f}\$ of 2V, I would expect the following:

Current across the resistor: \$I = \frac{(V-V_{f})}{R}\$ which means \$I = \frac{(10-2)}{1000}= 0.008A = 8 \text{mA}\$

So my resistor + LED draws 8 mA. Therefore the power dissipated by the resistor is \$P = IV = (0.008A)(8V)=0.064W\$

And the LED, which is drawing 8 mA,and has a \$V_{f} = 2 V\$ would dissipate \$(0.008A)(2V) = 0.016W\$

For a total power disspiation of 0.080W or 80 mW.

If I just have a 1kΩ resistor on the circuit I get a current of 10 mA, there's no voltage drop from anything else so 10 V is going across the resistor, and that means power is \$(0.010 A)(10V)=0.100W\$

So that says to me the resistor alone develops more power, though that seems oddly counterintuitive. On the other hand I am pretty sure power in a series circuit is additive, and on the third hand I know that with just a resistor, there's no voltage drops from anything else so you'd sort of expect that the resistor would be drawing more current since it's the only thing on the circuit.

Now if I add a resistor in parallel with the 1 kΩ one, say another 1kΩ, using the usual parallel resistance formula you'd have less resistance, you'd get 500 Ω and that would be 16 mA drawn by the resistor (and going into my LED). That gets you 128 mW from the resistor and 32 mW from the LED, for a total of 160 mW. Again, this tracks. If I have no LED on the circuit I get 500Ω with 10 V and that means 20 mA, which gets you a power dissipation of 200 mW.

I would like to know if any of the math or reasoning here is off, or if there is something I missed, or if a single element in a circuit (in series) really will draw less power as opposed to two or more elements.

title: Does this BJT transistor pair have a name? Perhaps "inverted Darlington"?
body:
I could not find another question exactly like this. What do we call the Q3/Q2 pair? It works like a Darlington, except in a Darlington both transistors have the same gender. So going from the base of Q3 to the collector of Q2, it appears that the (non-inverting) voltage gain is about

$$ G = \beta_{Q3} \cdot \beta_{Q2} \cdot \frac{R_6}{r_{Q3}} $$

where \$ r_{Q3} \$ is the base-emitter input impedance of Q3. The gain from the collector of Q1 to collector of Q2 appears to be

$$ G = \beta_{Q3} \cdot \beta_{Q2} \cdot \frac{R_6}{R_3+r_{Q3}} $$

which is much lower. Seems to me that R3 should be lower to make the amplifier hotter.

This is called "an op amp with three discrete transistors", but I would qualify that regarding the input impedance is very low. I think the whole thing can be made closer to a real op-amp by adding another NPN to the base of Q1 in a Darlington configuration. That would add another 0.7 volts changing the Zener D1 to be changed to something like a 1N5223B for 2.7 or 2.6 volts. This is to keep the DC value of the output and collector of Q2 to be about 4.0v to 4.5v, which is half of the power +Vcc.

But with a Darlington (or maybe an JFET input) to increase the input impedance, you can get a lotta gain and use this 4-transistor, 1 Zener circuit to be a pretty good op-amp that you can build either linear or non-linear computational blocks with. You could even turn the first stage (with Q1) into a sorta difference amp with the Zener replaced with a resistor. There would still be a way to negatively feedback the DC bias voltage (which should be circa 4.0 to 4.5 volts) with a feedback path to the inverting terminal input.

Does anyone know what C1 does? (Answered) It doesn't seem to do much LPFing at audio frequencies. Is it needed for stability? (Because the circuit doesn't look unstable to me without C1.)

I think I understand the circuit (there's nothing particularly fancy about it), but I am curious what that transistor pair is called. I can't find it in my half-century old Millman and Halkais textbook. We shoulda been taught this in my undergrad electronics class.

I recently finished an intro analog electronics course with flying colors, so I have been introduced to diodes and BJTs at a basic level. It was mostly amplification in the class, though, and I just turned my attention to wondering how TTL logic works.

I had a look at the datasheet for the SN74LS04 (Texas Instruments Inc. 2004) (I now know that LS means Low-Power Schottky), and turned to the page with the nominal non-Schottky BJT circuit. I have added some labels to the components so we may discuss on equal terms.

This is quite bizarre to me. I have learned about BJTs in terms of Common Collector/Base/Emitter or diode-connected configurations, in isolation, but I imagine these BJTs are not arranged as amplifiers, but to saturate as cleanly as possible.

I am aware that the most basic BJT inverter involves a single BJT pulling an output to ground when the BE junction is activated, with a pull-up resistor on the output to drive the output high when the junction is not activated. I kind of recognize the last stage of the circuit as a push-pull / totem-pole configuration, with that diode perhaps acting as a shoot-through / crossover mitigator when the output transitions?

  1. How does this circuit actually invert a signal. When the input is driven LOW, what chain of events from Q1 to Q2 to Q3/Q4 make the output source current so as to be pulled HIGH, and vice versa?

  2. How are the resistors calculated? How much does this matter for the logic to work?

  3. Why is everything NPN? I thought these circuits involved mixing of NPN and PNP, especially in the output stage.

  4. Why is this so much more complex than the simple single-BJT inverter one might imagine?

Thank you for your time.

title: Which method of adjusting the gain of an amplifier is better?
body:
Basically, all the volume control circuits, I have seen, have the following topology:

Here are two blocks. The first is voltage divider by RV1 with gain <=1. The second is opamp with constant gain 1 + R1/R2.

So, the volume control works like this: first we attenuate the signal, and then we amplify it. However, this leads to a decrease in the signal-to-noise ratio.

This raises a question for me: why don't people do as in the next schematic?

Here we can change the gain of the op amp from zero to RV1/R1 and maintain the signal-to-noise ratio. But obviously I'm missing something in this scheme, because people don't do that, at least I haven't seen it.

Comments about non-linearity control in 2nd scheme

Lets define:

$$ \gamma = \frac{RV_{1}(2, 3)}{RV_{1}(1, 3)} $$

Then gain in the 1st schematic will be:

$$ G_{1} = \frac{RV_{1}(2, 3)}{RV_{1}(1, 2) + RV_{1}(2, 3)}(1 + \frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}) = \gamma(1 + \frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}) $$

If we change the 2nd scheme, namely connecting RV1.1 and RV1.2, this will not change the concept, but will make the gain linear:

$$ G_{2} = \frac{RV_{1}(2, 3)}{R_{1}} = \gamma \frac{RV_{1}(1, 3)}{R_{1}} $$

As you can see, G1 and G2 is just factor of gamma, it means that above schematics are isomorphic by control gain.

title: Battery supply and tuning of a Bulova Accutron watch
body:

The watch is based on a tuning fork that is excited by an electronic tank circuit with 360 Hz frequency. You can't sleep when you wear this at night ;-)

My problem is that the watch circuit (i.e. frequency) is dependent on the original mercury battery voltage of 1.35V. This battery is hardly available these days. I would like to be able to use this watch with a modern 1.55V silver oxide battery, i.e. battery type 394.

The watch circuit principle is described in detail in the following paper (pages 10pp): Evolution of timekeeping from water clock to quartz clock - the curious case of the Bulova ACCUTRON 214 the first transistorized wristwatch

Quotation from that paper:

Should the battery be replaced with modern version at 1.55 V the higher oscillation amplitude and higher collector current can cause premature failure of the coils and tuning fork.

How can the circuit be modified to support a modern 1.55V battery?

I would also be happy to have a simulation model of the basic circuit, but I don’t know how to model the tuning fork or the CK722 transistor. Can I have some guidance for such a model (preferably in LTSpice or MicroCap)?

I measured the watch tuning fork frequency with a FFT app on my iPhone and compared a brand new 1.55V 394 type battery with a pretty drained one. Here is the result:

  • Varta V394 (drained): 1.378V, 5uA, f = 358 Hz
  • Maxell SR936SW (new): 1.598V, 5uA, f = 358 Hz

So it seems that the frequency does not change with battery voltage, which is great news!

title: What is the purpose of the neutral line in unbalanced three-phase systems?
body:
I keep seeing the same answer everywhere: "it's to complete the circuit and it also serves as a return path for current," but I have two problems with this:

  1. Why is it necessary to complete the circuit in a three-phase system? For single-phase systems I get it: if you don't complete the circuit no current will flow. But as far as I know, that is not the case with three-phase systems, where voltages between lines naturally occur as a result of the phase shift present between the generator voltages. I've even used an online simulator to confirm this. One possible explanation I could think of is that it "grounds" the load voltages, as in it makes sure that they won't surpass the peak voltage supplied by the generator. However, that wouldn't address the next point:
  2. Why does there need to be a path for "extra" current to return? I just don't get what that accomplishes. When I simulate a three-phase system with an unbalanced load, the "extra" current simply flows through the already existing wires, seemingly not causing anything weird to happen.

title: USB3 pass-through on a board - dealing with the USB-PD situation?
body:
We have a board where the customer wants to be able to pass USB through from one USB-C connector (on the back) to another (on the front) to make plugging in the odd peripheral easier - sounds easy right?

But, given the way USB has evolved now I believe we have to at least consider the possibility that someone plugs in devices that can provide/demand 100W or more of power, latest specs being up to 5A at up to 48V.

Now, on conforming equipment there are dedicated connectors (ports and plugs) with better contacts (possibly extra contacts (1)) and invariably a chip sitting behind them that does the relevant negotiations as source or sink - reading various appnotes and guides suggests that there's also intelligence in the higher power cables:

All USB-C cables are expected to support 20 V at 3 A for a total of 60 W. In order to be detected as capable of higher voltages and currents by the USB-PD controller, USB-C cables are required to contain a so-called e-marker chip which contains a vendor defined message (VDM) containing details on the cable and its capabilities.

But as "man in the middle", we are in an odd position - we are definitely on the end of a cable coming from the host, and probably with a 2nd cable between us and the device - either cable could be a "smart" or "dumb" one and whether we decide to be "smart" or "dumb" or pass through or interrupt the negotiations it seems this is a scenario the USB standard was not anticipating.

We don't really want to have to fit the full-fat 240W capable connectors etc. but also I can't see a simple way we can ensure that everything else plugged in won't negotiate its way up to >100W if we act purely as a dumb / transparent passthrough... unless the absence of the "good" connectors on our edges is enough to prevent the negotiation getting any further than the 60W stage?

I realise the full answer to this is to arrange an intravenous drip of caffeine and attempt to read the entire USB3.x spec from cover to leather-bound cover but hopefully someone here can spare me that fate.

(1) = Microchip Appnote AN18.25 suggests (in Table 1 / pg6) that PD-capable connectors & cables may have some extra pins and signalling over regular ones.

EDIT to add: Microchip appear to be going ham with USB-3 repeaters in this application, chaining 5 reclocker boards and 4 USB-C cables, I'm still reading to work out if this is in any way legal or alternatively what they've been smoking. Section 5 of the linked datasheet "EV23B43A TYPE-C REPEATER" shows the arrangement but they do employ a manual switch to change direction/orientation.

title: Potential problem when powering a cheap 8-bit MCU on moving/floating VDD & VSS voltages in an appliance; maintains (steady state) 5V difference
body:

The circuits get power from mains rectified, then voltage regulated using two zener diodes at VEE=24V and VCC=29V (5V above 24V) respectively.

The 5V MCU gets power from VCC with VSS connected to VEE, so a relative 5V. This looks fine to me.

What boggles me is that VEE is directly always connected to the 24V coil. How the MCU controls the energizing of the coil is via a transistor cascade which, when the MCU wants to deenergize the coil, shorts VEE to GND, which effectively bypasses the 24V zener diode, making VEE equal to GND thus without causing any serious shorts.

But now to the MCU, VCC now goes from seeing 29V&24V to seeing 5V&GND. Steady-state wise no problem I suppose, but the transients I am uncertain. Is this method standard? in what aspects is it better or worse than a typical cascade consisting of an NPN low side switch + PNP high side switch at the coil? Why would the designer want this? So far I can see that maybe it saves one or two resistors.

  3. added 330uF and 100nF between VCC and VEE.
  4. fixed 47uF between VEE and common instead of 330uF.

title: How does user-configurable SRAM/flash size work?
body:
AT32F435 is an ARM Cortex-M4F microcontroller. The datasheet claims "Default 384 Kbytes of SRAM, configurable up to maximum 512 Kbytes". Digging further, the reference manual says:

The AT32F435/437 series contain a 384-KB on-chip SRAM which starts at the address 0x2000_0000. It can be accessed by bytes, half-words (16 bits) or words (32 bits). In addition, AT32F435/437 also provide a special mode that enables a dynamic switch between 128 KB (minimum) and 512 KB (maximum). This is done by setting the EOPB0 bit. In 512 KB mode, Flash memory size (zero wait sate) is limited to 128 KB, while in 128 KB extension mode, the zero-wait-state Flash size is limited to 512 KB. On-chip SRAM is divided into SRAM1 and SRAM2. The SRAM1 is fixed at 64 KB, and can be accessed through either address 0x2000_0000~0x2000_FFFF or 0x1000_0000~0x1000_FFFF. The SRAM2 size ranges from 64 KB to 448 KB, accessible through address 0x2001_0000~2007_FFF.

Furthermore, it gives this table which implies that configuring for a larger SRAM shrinks your available flash space:

Although it is quite detailed in how to configure the flash/SRAM, neither the reference manual nor the datasheet explain what is going on under the hood. My question is: what is the mechanism in use here, and why does configuring for more SRAM shrink the available flash size?

title: How to design a common emitter amplifier for an 8Ω speaker?
body:
I was instructed to use a 2N2222 transistor to drive an 8Ω speaker, by using just a single stage.

I used a full-bypass capacitor for the emitter, but perhaps a partial bypass would make it easier to have a higher gain.
Here were my initial calculations:
For Vcc = 12 V, and peak power dissipation of the transistor taken to be 300 mW (well below the limit of 500 mW):
\$ V_{CEQ} = \frac{Vcc-V_{CE,SAT}}{2} +V_{CE,SAT}= \frac{12-0.4}{2} + 0.4 = 6.2 V \$
IC = P/V = 300/6.2 = 48.4 mA
IE = 48.4 mA
\$IC = \frac{Vcc- V_{CEQ}}{RE+RC} ~~\rightarrow ~~RE+RC=119.8 \$

Vcc/(RE+RC) is approximately double the IC value; IC of the Q-point lands in the middle of the I-V output characteristic curve, so it's not bad.
From what I see online, the gain is approximately RC/RE. For a modest gain of 20, I calculated RE and RC values.
Then I got \$V_E\$ to be about 0.2 V by knowing the emitter current and resistor. Then from \$V_{BE}\$ = 0.7 V, I calculated \$V_B\$ to be about 0.8 V.
This gives a relationship for the resistors in the voltage divider. I took the small one (RB2) to be 1k, and calculated RB1 from that.
I chose the same bypass capacitor value (4000) that I used in a power-transistor amplifier circuit.

I understand that my calculations are wrong due to not considering the high current through the load, thanks to some great videos by Aaron Danner. But his analytical-based explanations were not sufficient for me to understand how to approach my design problem.

title: Why does a changing voltage appear to pass through a capacitor?
body:
It's such a simple concept, yet one that's often oversimplified with the phrase, "Capacitors pass AC and block DC." Intuitively, though, I've never really understood why this happens.

I've run into a problem where, because I don't properly conceptualize this phenomenon, I struggle to recognize when and how to implement it naturally in my own circuit designs.

I'll mention a circuit where I've encountered this effect, but my main question is:
How should I conceptualize why a capacitor allows a changing voltage to pass through it?
This example is a pulse generator featured in The Art of Electronics (fig. 2.12 in 3rd edition). The explanation and operation of the circuit aren't particularly difficult to understand, but there's one thing I struggle with:
the node connected to Q2's base swings to a negative voltage. It's relatively easy to understand what's happening once you know that this negative voltage swing occurs. However, conceptually, I don't understand why a voltage swing from 5 V to ground on the left side of the capacitor would cause the node on its right side to swing negative. (I know it doesn't reach true ground because of (VCE(sat)), but that doesn't matter for this example.) I find this strange because I frequently encounter similar phenomena in circuits where capacitors allow voltages to rise above or fall below the supply rails, such as in bootstrapping circuits.

If I simply suspend my disbelief and accept that "capacitors pass AC and block DC," it's easy to say that the capacitor allows the changing voltage on one side to be superimposed on the voltage at the other node.

But that still doesn't explain why it happens, at least not in a way that makes intuitive sense to me.

What I'm really looking for is a physical and intuitive understanding of what's happening inside the capacitor and why a change in voltage on one plate causes the voltage on the other plate to change, sometimes even beyond the supply rails.

title: Would it be ideal to have non-overlapping threshold voltages for the NMOS and PMOS in this totem pole?
body:
In my beginners electronics course, we were learning about the very basic structure of a totem pole.

I had the circuit diagram below:

Where \$R=330\Omega\$, P is a potentiometer with variable resistance in the range \$[0, 10K\Omega]\$ and \$V=5V\$.

At first, I was wondering why a resistor would be wired in above the PMOS. Removing it would make the output voltage equal \$V\$ when the gate voltage is low, which sounded more ideal.

I wired up the circuit using a NMOS with minimum \$V_{th}=1.6V\$ and a PMOS with minumum \$V_{th}=-3.0V\$. The thresholds having these values meant both the NMOS and PMOS would be open simultaneously in certain voltage ranges and it would therefore flow a current from the drain of the PMOS to the drain of the NMOS. The highest current I could measure was \$I=8.5 \mu A\$ for \$V_{GA}=-3.23V\$ and \$V_{GB}=1.77V\$ as you can see below:

This explained why a resistor would be needed in this circuit. Removing it would cause a short circuit in certain voltage ranges.

Now say you had an NMOS with a minimum threshold voltage \$N_{th}=3V\$ and a PMOS with min threshold voltage \$P_{th}=-3V\$. Call the gate-source voltage of the NMOS \$V_N\$ and the gate-source voltage of the PMOS \$V_P\$. Would you not be able to remove the resistor as the NMOS would only conduct if \$V_N>N_{th} \iff V_G > N_{th} = 3V \$ and the PMOS would only conduct if \$V_P < P_{th} \iff V_G - V < P_{th} \iff V_G < -3V + 5V = 2V \$? That is, no gate voltage could open the MOSFETs simultaneously in this configuration. \$V_1=\$ voltage at node 1 (top of the dependent source).

Since the bottom of the \$6 \Omega\$ resistor is node 1 and the top is a, the current through the \$6 \Omega\$ resistor is: \$i_1 = \frac{V_a - V_1}{6}\$

The dependent current source provides: \$2i_1 = 2 \left( \frac{V_a - V_1}{6} \right)\$

The resistance:

\$R_{ab} = \frac{V_a}{I_{\text{a}}} = \frac{V_a}{V_a \cdot \frac{25}{84}} = \frac{84}{25} = 3.36\,\Omega\$

title: Does MOSFET-based polarity protection work with single alkaline cells?
body:
There are various ways to protect against reverse polarity when installing batteries. For example, one possibility is a diode. Unfortunately, diodes have a high voltage drop, sometimes even the voltage drop of a Schottky diode is too high.

Another possibility is for example a P-channel MOSFET with its drain connected to positive battery terminal and gate connected to negative battery terminal. Then if the voltage of a single alkaline cell is 1.0 volts for example (at the end of its useful life), the source of the MOSFET has a voltage of 0.3 volts or above (before the MOSFET turns on, assuming silicon P-N diode drop of 0.7 volts or below, more likely below since the current is so low at this stage), and the gate is at 0 volts, so the source-to-gate voltage is somewhat above (in absolute value) to minus 0.3 volts (before the MOSFET turns on).

Are there any MOSFETs capable of working in this manner, with a source-to-gate voltage of minus 0.3 volts (or slightly more) turning the MOSFET gradually on? Of course, once the MOSFET is gradually turned on, then the source voltage begins to rise and eventually the source-to-gate voltage reaches minus 1.0 volts which might allow even significant current without too much resistive drop.

I understand for example that modern CMOS microprocessors operate with very low voltages. So clearly such MOSFETs that could be used for reverse polarity protection with a single alkaline cell might exist. But do such MOSFETs exist as discrete components? Can I buy one?

At least there are logic level MOSFETs which are fully turned on with source-to-gate voltage of 3.3 volts, but with a single alkaline cell, the voltages are much lower than that.

EDIT: Microchip responded that this is an error in the datasheet.

We have received clarification from our technical experts regarding the 16-bit register access order in the ATtiny102/104. After a thorough review, it has been confirmed that the datasheet contains a bug. Despite the documentation stating otherwise, the correct way to access 16-bit registers in the ATtiny102/104 is to write the high byte first, then the low byte—consistent with other AVR devices.

Please kindly disregard our previous comment indicating that the order was intentional. Your feedback has directly contributed to us catching and addressing this error. Additionally, our team has identified a few other areas in the datasheet where contradictory information about 16-bit register access exists and we are taking steps to log and correct these documentation errors to ensure future accuracy.

ORIGINAL QUESTION:

The ATtiny102 datasheet says on access the 16-bit registers:

Note:  To perform a 16-bit write operation, the low byte must be written before the high byte. For a 16-bit read, the low byte must be read before the high byte.

(read and write both going in the order LOW->HIGH)

However, every other AVR datasheet I’ve checked shows the opposite order for writes. ATtiny5, another AVRrc core:

To do a 16-bit write, the high byte must be written before the low byte. For a 16-bit read, the low byte must be read before the high byte

ATmega328P:

To do a 16-bit write, the high byte must be written before the low byte. For a 16-bit read, the low byte must be read before the high byte.

Another doc, AVR072: Accessing 16-bit I/O Registers:

Note that the read and the write operation differ in the order the high and low I/O Register is accessed. If the order is reversed, the high value will be incorrectly read or written.

(reads are LOW->HIGH and writes are HIGH->LOW)

title: Quadrature vs. pulse-counting detector

I am attempting to construct the circuitry of a LaserDisc player. LaserDisc, for those who are unaware, is/was an analog optical disc video storage format. The player then uses traditional optical disc drive technology to read the data and then filters, demodulates, and amplifies the video signal for output to a CRT TV.

I have found some circuit diagrams online, but have run into a problem. It is not with the chips being outdated—the basic video demodulation part of the circuitry appears to use chips which are still being made today (as far as I can tell). It is with the type of detector used to demodulate the signal.

An optical disc will inevitably have “dropouts”—pieces of the disc’s data which are not read due to a variety of reasons—which, on a LaserDisc, appear as missing horizontal lines on the TV. The player takes advantage of the close similarity of adjacent lines to fix this—if a dropout is detected, it simply inserts the line adjacent to the one being scanned in place of the missing line. This is done by sending a copy of the signal through a 64-microsecond delay line.

However, this takes place before the signal is demodulated, and the demodulation takes place in a different way on each copy of the signal. The regular copy is demodulated via a pulse-counting detector, while the delayed copy is passed through a quadrature detector.

My question, therefore, is this: what are the advantages and disadvantages of each detector type compared to each other? And, more importantly, could I replace the pulse-counting detector with a quadrature detector (assuming the circuitry was sufficiently altered)? (The quadrature circuit uses a chip which is still being made today, while the pulse-counting circuit uses an IF amp which is not produced today and would likely be more expensive to implement.)

title: How well would a hypothetical electric grid with no inertial at all work?

Would that be less bad or worse than a frequency drop in a regular grid? If it would be unworkable, would batteries be enough to fix that? title: Creating an RMS multimeter without specialized chips – How to do it?
body:
I am currently brainstorming ideas for an DIY multimeter. I’d really like it to be able to measure the true RMS (or at least very close to) voltage of what’s connected to its input. Usually, this is done with a dedicated LSI, but I’ve got an idea on how I could potentially do it without the usual complex circuitry and specialised parts.

Below, you can see a simplified sketch of my idea. Right now, I’m mostly concerned with the theory, hence all parts and blocks drawn here are ideal, magical parts with no flaws.

The basic idea is as follows:

We rectify the input signal using a precision rectifier, this produces a full-wave rectified output whose peak voltage is identical to that of the input (no voltage drops, no distortions – it’s ideal).

We then feed this rectified signal into an integrator. Because the integrator’s input is always positive, we accumulate charge in the capacitor, while counting how much time does it take for the integrator output voltage to reach some known threshold.

Of course, in the real world, such a single-slope integrator ADC comes with quite a few problems (plus is impractical form a logic design stand point as we need to count down instead of up), but here in magical theory land, it should be sufficient to prove the idea as sound.

With an DC input voltage, the circuit behaves as if the rectifier isn’t there, and we’re simply accumulate charge in the integrator at a constant rate.

To test this idea, I had to simulate it, I used falstad to do it as I am unfamiliar with LTSpice or any other programs.

I’ll only present the time it took for each waveform to reach the threshold voltage, since the component values and exact voltages are irrelevant here, as they remained the same for all tests.

All waveforms started from 0 degrees, (i.e. 0V for sine and triangle), all were set to the same RMS voltage as the DC control.

  • DC Control: 99.985ms
  • Triangle Wave: 99.99ms
  • Sine Wave: 111.515ms

As you can see, while the triangle wave is super close, hovering around what I’d consider a measurement error, the sine wave took quite a bit longer to reach the threshold voltage.

I thought about how the frequency of the input signal would cause some error, as if the frequency is too low for the input waveform to complete a full cycle over the integration time, we’d get an inaccurate result.

In this case the AC waveforms were set to 100Hz, which gives us 10 cycles per integration time.

Additionally, we have the issue where the rate of change in the output voltage is constantly fluctuating for the AC waveforms. Let’s take a worst case scenario where we try to measure the RMS voltage of a pulse wave with 1% duty cycle. For 99% of the cycle the integrator output voltage wouldn’t change at all, only to rapidly rise during the short on-time. Getting an accurate measurement of such a signal would be very difficult, unless we could maybe integrate over 100 cycles of the input waveform or so.

I’d like to hear some feedback from the many knowledgable people here, is my approach a complete dead-end, or do I have something here that could potentially be improved.

I’d also like to ask how to the ready-made RMS converter LSIs overcome the afford mentioned frequency issue? I am designing my meter to only use logic chips, so a microcontroller digitally adjusting and refining the measured value over a long period of time isn’t really an option.

title: How is the Miller plateau related to the Miller effect?
body:
Is the Miller plateau in MOSFET switching actually caused by the Miller effect?

I'm trying to understand the relationship between these two concepts given their names seem to suggest they are somewhat related.

In small-signal analysis, for a common-source amplifier, \$C_{GD}\$ appears as a Miller capacitance because the Miller effect multiplies it by \$(1+A_v)\$, making it more significant at the input. That part to me is clear.

What confuses me is how the Miller effect relates to the Miller plateau during switching. As I understand it, the plateau arises because the gate drive current must discharge \$C_{GD}\$ from \$(V_{DS} - V_{GP})\$ to \$-V_{GP}\$. During this time, \$V_{GS}\$ remains roughly constant, producing the characteristic flat region on the gate voltage waveform.

If the plateau is genuinely a consequence of the Miller effect, I would expect the voltage gain to play a direct role in its duration. But in practice, what seems to matter most is the magnitude of \$V_{DS}\$, not the transconductance or drain current which influence \$V_{GP}\$ but do not affect the duration of the plateau in a significant way.

Also, if we use an NMOS as a high-side switch with the drain connected to \$V_{DD}\$ and source left open, theoretically there should be very little gain but that doesn't seem to affect the Miller plateau.

Is the name "Miller plateau" just a loose analogy or is there a more rigorous connection to the Miller effect that I'm missing?

title: How does this delay line travel faster than light?
body:
Board design:

Fab: 1.6mm thick substrate, εr ~ 4.8, seems to be normal FR-4 stock. (I actually measure more like ~5.3, but I don't have very good mechanical tolerances in the measurement, and it's only a low-frequency figure.) 0.56mm width trace should be close to 100Ω Z0 (not that fab tolerances are great here, either; but neither does Z0 vary all that quickly). Circuit is a dual single-balanced mixer to generate quadrature outputs. There are 1:1+1 baluns (L7-L9, L16-L18; pads provided by some 1210 footprints crudely overlaid as I don't need to make proper footprints or models for this project), BAS70-07 dual diodes (D1, D2), some damping resistance (R8/R15, 470Ω), and a 3rd-order diplexing filter (right half). (Grounds provided by vias, or copper foil wrapped around board edge. Bottom side is 100% contiguous.)

(Balun cores are similar to Fair-Rite 2861002702, and windings are 2t 28AWG each.)

Reference input is at the bottom-middle, by R14. Source is a tuned amplifier, delivering about 10dBm into 50Ω, at 300MHz.

Signal input is at the center-right, by R13. Source is wideband amplifier, in the -10 to 0dBm range. Tone is variable, in this case shifted by a couple MHz relative to ref.

As frequency is fairly high, I opted for a delay line to obtain phase shift. One full cycle of 300MHz is 3.33ns; a quarter is 0.833ns, and at c ~ 56% c0, 140mm should be required. Ideally, this generates quadrature, or a bit past, really (I designed in extra, expecting to cut it down as needed).
